# Relays and Distribution

How one publication reaches many people without becoming many publications.

If every viewer needs a separate copy directly from the lecturer, the lecturer’s upload becomes the audience limit. A relay moves the copying work into the distribution network.

## A relay plays both roles

A relay is a subscriber toward an upstream source and a publisher toward downstream subscribers. It terminates transport connections and handles MoQ metadata. It is more than a router forwarding encrypted IP packets.

```{=html}
<figure class="flow"><div class="flow-nodes"><div><span class="node-icon">01</span><strong>Publisher</strong><span>Creates objects</span></div><span class="connector" aria-hidden="true">→</span><div><span class="node-icon">02</span><strong>Relay</strong><span>Forwards objects</span></div><span class="connector" aria-hidden="true">→</span><div><span class="node-icon">03</span><strong>Subscribers</strong><span>Choose their tracks</span></div></div><figcaption>One publisher. A shared relay. Each viewer receives the tracks they request.</figcaption></figure>
```

With several interested viewers, a relay can share upstream content and forward it to each downstream connection. If a second relay is closer to another audience, it can repeat that pattern. A network of these relationships provides distribution across regions.

This does not eliminate bandwidth costs. If a relay sends a two-megabit-per-second track to 100 viewers, the payload egress is roughly 200 megabits per second, before overhead. The benefit is sharing the upstream path and placing fan-out where capacity is available.

## Caching helps, but has limits

A caching relay can hold recently received objects. A new viewer may obtain a useful group without waiting for the original publisher to send it again. Immutable object identities let different viewers reuse the same cached payload.

MOQT permits caching; it does not require every relay to store every object. Even a caching relay has a retention policy and finite memory. Never infer that an accepted live subscription includes an unlimited archive.

For the lecture, retaining a few useful recent groups may improve startup. Keeping the entire class for replay is a separate storage feature with different costs and lifetime requirements.

## Each hop has its own conditions

The lecturer’s connection can be fast while one viewer’s connection is slow. A relay has to make downstream delivery decisions for each path. Slowing every viewer to match the slowest one would defeat the point of independent subscriptions.

This is also why “the stream has low latency” is incomplete. Which subscriber? Which path? Which queue? A nearby viewer and a distant viewer may have very different experiences of the same publication.

Measure at the edges, then trace through the hops. A healthy publisher-to-relay connection says little about a congested relay-to-viewer connection.

## Relays need structure, not codec knowledge

A relay uses names, group boundaries, priorities, and delivery rules. It need not inspect the encoded picture to forward it. That separation makes a generic relay useful for audio, video, and application data.

It also means the publisher must describe content honestly. If a supposed join point actually depends on an earlier group, the relay cannot repair the mistake by looking at a label. Format design and encoder behavior must agree.

## What a relay does not automatically do

Forwarding a high-resolution track does not create a low-resolution version. A **transcoder** decodes and re-encodes media; a relay distributes the objects it receives. A service can run both roles, but they are different jobs.

Likewise, DNS routing, selecting a nearby relay, arranging redundancy, and recovering application state are deployment choices. The moq.dev project supplies clustering features; they should not be mistaken for a universal, automatic global MoQ network.

Before scaling the lecture, draw the actual publisher, relay, and viewer paths. Mark where content is cached and where authorization is checked. That small drawing often reveals more than a single “CDN” box.
